lessons.title: Networking and energy: bound work and keep results fresh
lessons.summary: Treat transfer, decoding, disk work, and queues as separate costs. Limit work, choose cache and cancellation rules, and check device energy under declared conditions.
objectives: Separate network wait, CPU transformation, queue delay, and cache lookup cost.
Limit active and waiting work without blocking Swift's cooperative task execution.
Explain the differences between dropping buffered values, slowing a producer, limiting concurrent work, and limiting requests per second.
Choose cache and energy experiments that preserve freshness, account scope, and cancellation.

sections.title: Follow the whole request, not just the transfer
sections.html:
A request pipeline is the chain from asking for data to using it. URLSession handles transport, but the feature may also wait in a queue, prepare a request, decode bytes, build rows, write to disk, and present content. Android OkHttp calls have a similar surrounding chain. Time the stages needed for your hypothesis. A fast download is not proof of fast usable content. A cache hit avoids some transfer while still possibly doing expensive parsing or image decoding. Name the stage before deciding which operation is slow.

URLSessionTaskMetrics can provide transaction information such as timing and resource-fetch context where available. Connection reuse, protocol, redirects, and cache decisions affect interpretation. Some phase timestamps can be absent or overlapping; do not fill missing values with zero or pretend each request creates a new DNS lookup. A task can include multiple transactions. Coordinate metrics collection with the actual session/delegate arrangement rather than adding a new session per request just to get callbacks.

The active dispatcher injects a data-task provider and preserves cancellation before reachability error mapping. This is a production seam, not a benchmark result. Its data(for:) contract returns complete Data, so account for buffering and decode memory. The streaming path has a different resource and lifetime contract. Choose between them from payload and consumer requirements, not because streaming sounds inherently faster. Transfer size, latency, CPU, memory, and energy are related but independent outcomes.

sections.title: Limit both the work running and the work waiting
sections.html:
A concurrency limit caps how many operations may be active at once. It does not automatically cap queued tasks or their memory. Lesson 015 seeds a task group with a small window and adds one child when another completes. This limits initially created children as well as active ones. Starting ten thousand tasks that wait for a permit can retain ten thousand sets of captured data and waiting state. State a waiting-work budget and a payload-byte budget as well as the active count.

Task-group results arrive in completion order. Include the input index and let only the parent write ordered output slots. An error escaping the group body cancels and joins remaining children, but their operations must cooperate. Preserve both transport cancellation and CancellationError. Check cancellation before adding replacement work and before publication. A group limit cannot force a blocking or unresponsive legacy operation to stop.

A parallelism limit is not a requests-per-second rate limit. Three quick requests can generate many requests in one second. URLSession connection limits also do not directly cap application tasks, decode workers, or multiplexed requests under every protocol. Pick independent limits for network demand, decode work, and disk operations when evidence supports that separation. Choose the numbers by comparing throughput, tail latency, memory peak, and contention on representative devices, not by copying CPU count into every resource policy.

sections.title: A small buffer may drop values instead of slowing input
sections.html:
Backpressure means demand or capacity can slow production. Buffering means holding values until a consumer uses them. AsyncSequence describes asynchronous iteration, but does not promise that every producer waits for its consumer. A callback-based AsyncStream may receive data faster than it is consumed. Default unbounded buffering can grow. .bufferingNewest(1) keeps at most one waiting value by dropping older ones; it does not suspend the producer. Limiting the element count also does not bound bytes if one element can hold a huge payload.

Choose loss policy from semantics. Progress snapshots can often be replaced by newer snapshots. Ordered text tokens, booking commands, or dependent deltas cannot be arbitrarily dropped. A lossless pipeline needs a demand-aware channel, pull-based source, bounded transport/parser stages, or explicit overflow failure with recovery. Record starts, buffered bytes, drops, termination, and consumption without logging sensitive payload. The Kotlin Flow analogy is helpful for thinking about collectors, but a callback bridge does not automatically inherit Flow's suspension semantics.

The checkout's streaming factory retains a Task and cancels it in onTermination. Follow that cancellation through parser and transport; source wiring alone is not proof of prompt termination on every path. The existing byte-forwarding benchmark constructs many bytes and forwards them individually. Its harness can expose overhead, but does not reproduce cellular transport, server pacing, or UI consumption. Inspect buffering and parser work separately before choosing a chunking change.

sections.title: An async wrapper can still block on a file
sections.html:
Blocking work occupies its execution thread until it finishes. A synchronous Foundation file read does work in the caller's context. Adding async to a wrapper does not convert the file operation into nonblocking I/O. Keep those reads out of body, cell configuration, and MainActor callbacks. A legacy blocking adapter needs a deliberately bounded execution arrangement and safe result transfer. Do not block a cooperative task thread on a semaphore while waiting for another task. Also separate file reading from parsing and publication when investigating the cause.

Distinguish reading bytes, decoding a snapshot, querying a database, writing a temporary file, and atomically replacing the intended file. Atomic replacement protects a publication boundary under the API's contract; it is not a universal promise that every byte is durable through power loss. Cache data and user-authored drafts have different durability, backup, and protection requirements. Temporary failures, protected-data unavailability, missing files, and corruption need different outcomes.

Batch small writes or coalesce replaceable state when product semantics allow it. Do not debounce a critical user save into loss without an explicit flush/lifetime policy. A backgrounded app may have limited execution opportunity. Avoid reserializing unchanged large snapshots or writing an entire cache after every element. Warm file caches can hide I/O cost in repeated local runs; compare declared states and actual device behavior. A reduced write count is mechanism evidence, while battery benefit still requires an appropriate energy experiment.

sections.title: Name what makes a cached result still valid
sections.html:
A cache key identifies a reusable result. Include the account or scope, endpoint and parameters, locale when relevant, image size, and source version as the result requires. Freshness says when the stored result remains acceptable. Define expiry or validation, capacity, eviction, stored errors, and logout behavior. A dictionary that never evicts trades fewer requests for growing memory. An actor protects isolated access; it is not a dedicated thread and does not make a bad key correct. Race-free code can still return stale data or another account's result.

The current AsyncCache separates eviction from invalidation. evictAll() removes stored values while allowing in-flight results to refill them. invalidateAll() also advances a generation, a revision number that rejects older cache commits. That does not necessarily stop transport or stop an existing caller receiving an old value. The feature still needs its own check before showing that result. Read both checks and keep eviction, cache invalidation, consumer relevance, and cancellation as different decisions.

HTTP caching through URLCache has protocol freshness and validation behavior; an application object cache has domain semantics. Avoid independently serving stale authenticated data just because both layers report hits. The application initializer clears shared URL responses, so a proposed persistence optimization must account for that actual policy. Cache-hit rate alone is not success: measure saved transfers, lookup CPU, disk operations, retained bytes, freshness failures, and latency under eviction. A cold or invalidated cache must remain functionally correct.

sections.title: Choose who owns a request with several waiters
sections.html:
Coalescing means sharing one operation for identical requests. It can save duplicate transfer or decoding, but it creates a service-owned lifetime. If waiter A leaves while B still needs the result, decide whether work continues. If all waiters leave, choose cancellation, public-cache completion, or another explicit policy. Cancellation is a request and needs cooperation. Awaiting an unstructured Task's value does not automatically pass a waiter's cancellation to that task. The service must keep separate consumer interests and operation ownership.

Account transitions need an independent generation or scope guard. Invalidate old pending commits so a late request cannot refill the new account's cache. Also prevent a now-obsolete UI caller from publishing an old result. These are two guards at different boundaries. Test logout during transfer, replacement query during decode, and cancellation while waiting for a permit using controlled fake gates. Random sleeps can hide the interleaving you actually need to prove.

A limit on requests does not solve priority inversion. Visible content can wait behind large speculative prefetches. Reserve capacity or prioritize demand according to a documented scheduler policy, and cancel obsolete speculative work. Task priority is a scheduling hint rather than a fairness guarantee. Reuse an appropriate URLSession and provider so connection state and middleware stay coherent. Creating fresh sessions or bypassing protection to make a benchmark faster changes the product's security and transport contract.

sections.title: Reduce optional work when resources are under pressure
sections.html:
Resource pressure means heat, power policy, or scarce memory should affect the work admitted by a service. Imagine visible search results, speculative pages, and image thumbnails sharing workers. More concurrency can heat the device, raise memory peaks, or delay the next visible request. Keep required user work separate from safe-to-delay speculation. One service policy should make these choices; every cell need not poll the device independently. Android power and thermal APIs offer similar design questions, but their signals and thresholds are not exact iOS counterparts.

ProcessInfo reports thermalState as nominal, fair, serious, or critical. Read the initial state and observe thermalStateDidChangeNotification for later changes. Define how worsening heat reduces expendable work; critical pressure may require stopping power-intensive work. isLowPowerModeEnabled is separate: it describes power-saving mode, not temperature or battery percentage. A service may reduce optional downloads or movement using these inputs. Neither signal grants more background time. Move notification handling into the service's isolation domain before changing its scheduler.

Memory warnings are a different pressure signal. UIKit provides delegate/controller callbacks and didReceiveMemoryWarningNotification. Release reconstructible data and curb expensive allocations promptly rather than scanning an entire ownership graph while already under pressure. Warnings are best-effort; termination can occur without time for cleanup. Maintain budgets and normal durable-save policy before a warning instead of depending on one final callback. Clearing an image cache cannot release a bitmap still strongly retained by a visible cell. Simulator warning injection exercises a reaction path, not a phone's real memory ceiling.

Write a fixture matrix for normal, low-power, elevated-thermal and memory-pressure inputs. For each row specify admission of new speculative work, treatment of in-flight work, visible-content fallback and recovery. Use fake conditions and gated completions to verify policy deterministically. When conditions improve, resume through a bounded queue rather than launching every deferred item simultaneously. Preserve account-generation and cancellation checks: a resource-policy change must not publish a stale result or convert a failed save into success. A physical-device observation separately records conditions, responsiveness, peak memory and the actual mechanism counts. The fixture proves decisions; it does not prove battery savings, absence of thermal throttling or safe production limits.

sections.title: Count repeated work as well as individual waits
sections.html:
Energy is the work that draws on the battery over an observation window. It is not identical to request latency or CPU time. Repeated timers, retries, tiny transfers, and wakeups can keep resources active. Group compatible work, avoid duplicate bytes, reuse suitable connections, and request media at useful sizes. These are mechanisms to investigate, not measured battery savings. Compression spends CPU to save transfer bytes. Disk caching spends writes to avoid later transfer. Compare relevant phone and network conditions before choosing which tradeoff helps.

Use available energy/power tools on a supported physical device and retain tool version and capabilities. A simulator and a single stopwatch cannot supply phone energy evidence. Hold the observation window, workload, connectivity, display conditions, and background policy constant. Separate mechanism counts such as wakeups, transfers, bytes, and CPU from an actual energy or power observation. Archived Apple energy guidance explains enduring mechanisms, but its older reachability code is not a mandate to preflight every request or a current implementation recipe.

Retries need deadlines, bounded attempts, cancellation, jitter when appropriate, and idempotency rules. Repeatedly retrying an unsafe mutation can duplicate effects even if it improves success-rate statistics. Low Power Mode and constrained or expensive network access require explicit product policy, not silent broken behavior. Measure tail latency, freshness, error rate, memory peak, and energy together for the intended operation. A successful optimization preserves the user's outcome while reducing a demonstrated cost.

quiz.question: You create 10,000 tasks, but only three may hold a permit. What is still unbounded by that permit?
options: The number of queued tasks and their retained captures.
Only the number of CPUs in the phone.
Nothing; all memory is capped at three elements.
quiz.explanation: An active-work permit does not bound already-created tasks or payloads. Windowed task creation also limits that queue.

quiz.question: Does bufferingNewest(1) provide lossless backpressure for ordered SSE deltas?
options: Yes, yield suspends automatically.
No, it can discard buffered values and does not suspend the producer.
Yes, as long as the consumer runs on MainActor.
quiz.explanation: A buffer policy can limit storage by dropping values. Ordered dependent deltas require a different lossless or explicit-overflow contract.

quiz.question: What does the active AsyncCache generation invalidation establish?
options: All pending transports are killed immediately.
Every waiter forgets the old response.
Older completions cannot repopulate that cache generation; cancellation and UI publication remain separate.
quiz.explanation: The generation guards cache commits. It does not itself define transport stopping or whether an existing caller may receive a result.

exercise.solution:
This standalone Swift window limits how many child tasks are created at once. It returns String snapshots that satisfy Sendable, the contract for safe transfer across concurrency boundaries. That window does not limit final output size, requests per second, or bytes in each payload. Give those separate rules in the harness. Keep cancellation cooperative and preserve input order with parent-owned result slots. The code supplies a bounded-work design, not evidence that any particular limit is fastest or saves battery.

enum WindowError: Error { case invalidLimit, incomplete }

func windowed(
    _ ids: [String], limit: Int,
    load: @escaping @Sendable (String) async throws -> String
) async throws -> [String] {
    guard limit > 0 else { throw WindowError.invalidLimit }
    try Task.checkCancellation()
    return try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: (Int, String).self) { group in
        var output = [String?](repeating: nil, count: ids.count)
        var next = 0
        for _ in 0..<min(limit, ids.count) {
            let index = next
            let id = ids[index]
            next += 1
            group.addTask {
                try Task.checkCancellation()
                return (index, try await load(id))
            }
        }
        while let (index, value) = try await group.next() {
            try Task.checkCancellation()
            output[index] = value
            if next < ids.count {
                let index = next
                let id = ids[index]
                next += 1
                group.addTask {
                    try Task.checkCancellation()
                    return (index, try await load(id))
                }
            }
        }
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        return try output.map { value in
            guard let value else { throw WindowError.incomplete }
            return value
        }
    }
}

@escaping allows the loader to be retained by child closures; @Sendable constrains captures. Only the parent writes optional output slots. One completion frees one position in the active window before a replacement is added. The final map refuses a missing result instead of using compactMap to silently publish fewer items.

Use gates to complete the third input first and prove input ordering. Cancel the outer task with children waiting, release/cancel fake gates, and verify no replacement or UI commit occurs after the relevant checks. A fake must cooperate or the structured scope will wait for it. Keep a service-owned generation for cache commits and a feature-owned generation for visible publication. Compare fixed workloads at each limit on the same device; do not infer an optimal number or energy improvement from this code alone.

lessons.title: Builds and algorithms: improve the bottleneck you can prove
lessons.summary: Measure build waiting and app work separately. Help type inference, inspect dependency chains, and replace repeated searching only when the output rules stay the same.
objectives: Define clean, incremental, and unchanged builds with the same tools and cache rules.
Explain type-checking work and required dependency chains separately from app runtime speed.
Compare algorithm growth, hashing, equality, memory, and output order.
Treat module and compiler changes as tradeoffs that need evidence.

sections.title: A faster build and a faster app are different results
sections.html:
Build elapsed time is the developer's wait for a product to compile. Runtime cost is the work the product does when launched or used. A rewrite may help Swift infer types without changing runtime behavior. An optimization flag may speed runtime but slow compilation. Keep separate experiments for these outcomes. Android compilation, annotation processing, resources, and dependency resolution offer familiar categories. Swift has its own compiler and module rules, so use the categories to ask questions rather than assuming the same flags or costs.

Define a clean build, an incremental build after a specified edit, and a no-op build with no inputs changed. Each measures a different workflow. A clean build in an isolated output location can still reuse package downloads or shared module caches unless you specify otherwise. A no-op build may unexpectedly run scripts that lack declared inputs and outputs. An incremental edit to a widely imported public contract can invalidate more work than the same edit inside an implementation.

Record revision, Xcode/compiler, SDK, selected scheme/destination/configuration, package resolution, host, competing jobs, and cache preparation. Don't compare a fresh dependency download against a candidate with everything installed. Retain timing summaries and logs, not just the terminal's total. Use matched batches when comparing changes. Build performance is reproducible only when you define the inputs and the reset boundary as carefully as a device benchmark.

sections.title: Find the dependency chain that holds up the build
sections.html:
A build timeline shows when jobs run and what waits for what. Xcode reports can separate compilation, module emission, linking, resources, signing, and scripts. Module emission produces the information other code needs to import a module. Linking combines compiled code into a product. The longest single job is not necessarily the whole critical path, the required chain that determines finish time. A long independent job can overlap others. Summed task durations can exceed elapsed time because jobs run together. Inspect dependencies as well as the duration list.

Inspect scripts for declared inputs and outputs and legitimate dependency requirements. A script that runs every time may be correct for its purpose; removing it without understanding code generation or validation changes the build contract. Conversely, an undeclared generator dependency can produce stale outputs despite an apparently fast incremental build. Verify both reproducibility and correctness. Never make deletion of every developer cache the default “optimization”; isolated experiments are easier to interpret and preserve unrelated work.

Module count introduces tradeoffs. Splitting a monolith can improve parallelism and isolate edits, but adds module overhead, dependencies, public surface, and integration work. A shared utility imported everywhere can create a wide invalidation boundary. The active ZDUI target depends on several internal products and mixed-language infrastructure, providing a real graph to inspect. Its list alone does not establish a measured bottleneck or authorize dependency removal.

sections.title: Give the compiler useful intermediate types
sections.html:
Type inference means the compiler works out types from expressions and context. Swift's type checker may explore many choices in overloaded operations, generic calls, closures, and view builders. A large ambiguous expression can make that search expensive. When diagnostics identify it, split the expression into meaningful stages with explicit intermediate types. A new local name alone may not reduce the inference problem. Keep the same result rules. The rankedIDs example below exposes filtering and ordering without promising a measured build improvement or a runtime speedup.

struct RankedItem {
    let id: String
    let score: Int
}
func rankedIDs(_ items: [RankedItem]) -> [String] {
    let eligible: [RankedItem] = items.filter { $0.score > 0 }
    let ordered: [RankedItem] = eligible.sorted { lhs, rhs in
        if lhs.score != rhs.score { return lhs.score > rhs.score }
        return lhs.id < rhs.id
    }
    return ordered.map { $0.id }
}

The type annotations tell the compiler the intermediate arrays' types and give each stage a name. lhs and rhs are just closure parameter names. The comparator orders higher scores first, then uses ID order for ties. filter and sorted still do runtime work and allocate; clearer inference is not a runtime measurement. Do not subtract scores to compare them, because subtraction can overflow and break the ordering rule.

Compiler diagnostic flags and timings vary by version. Use supported local diagnostics deliberately, record the exact command/toolchain, and keep temporary investigation flags out of permanent shared settings unless a separate requirement justifies them. A type-checker timeout is useful evidence about a source expression, not a reason to disable correctness checks.

sections.title: Read tools version, language mode, and deployment separately
sections.html:
A toolchain is the compiler and related tools actually running the build. swift-tools-version:5.9 states a package manifest's minimum tooling and interpretation requirements. It does not pin every compiler to 5.9, set all target language modes, or choose the oldest supported OS. Language mode controls Swift language rules; deployment target controls supported OS availability. The checkout's Tuist helper sets SWIFT_VERSION to 6 for selected targets. Other routes have their own settings. Read generated and effective settings for the build you measure, not one convenient header.

Debug builds commonly favor inspectability over runtime optimization. Release configurations may use speed or size choices and whole-module compilation. Whole-module optimization can enable cross-file analysis within a module but has compilation and incremental tradeoffs. Cross-module optimization depends on visibility, compiler choices, and resilience. Avoid blanket @inlinable additions: they expose implementation for client optimization and create API/compatibility obligations. Public interface design should not be distorted for an unmeasured small call.

Generics may enable specialization; existential values provide runtime abstraction and can involve indirection or boxing depending on representation. Dynamic dispatch and ARC costs may matter in a hot loop, but replacing every protocol or class with a concrete struct is not a sound default. Identify a hot path in an optimized binary, preserve dependency and isolation contracts, then compare representative inputs. Package pins establish dependency identity, not the newest docs, newest tools, or the effective settings of every build variant.

sections.title: Keep the output rule while reducing repeated searching
sections.html:
Stable deduplication removes repeated IDs while keeping the first occurrence order. A baseline can scan its growing output with contains for every input. With many distinct IDs, that can mean quadratic worst-case comparisons: the search grows as the output grows. A Set-backed candidate typically gives expected linear membership work across the input, with extra memory. Linear here does not mean every identifier costs the same amount. String hashing and equality depend on content. Lesson 023 introduced this example; now preserve order, equality, and duplicate choice while investigating its cost.

The active Sequence helper already uses a Set plus an ordered array. Its closure chooses the key for each item. Check that projection and order before creating another helper. An expensive key projection can matter even when membership improves. Changing equality, case folding, or Unicode normalization changes which items count as duplicates. These are behavior decisions, not interchangeable shortcuts. Swift String equality is not merely a comparison of raw bytes.

Compare fixtures with all unique, all equal, mixed duplicates, long strings, and realistic ordering. Measure several sizes to see growth, and avoid extrapolating one microbenchmark to the whole screen. Keep result order, duplicate choice, and error semantics fixed. A faster unordered Set conversion fails stable-order acceptance. Reserve capacity can reduce reallocations but may retain excess memory; choose it from expected sizes and measured tradeoffs rather than preallocating a maximum imaginable dataset.

sections.title: Check both algorithms produce the same full array
sections.html:
The standalone functions below take synthetic strings and keep the first occurrence of each. scanningUnique searches the output collected so far. indexedUnique also keeps a Set for membership and appends new strings to an ordered array. Two implementations let the harness check equivalent results before timing. Neither should sort or change case. The shape mirrors the active Sequence helper without claiming a production change. Compare complete arrays, including order, rather than just counting the returned elements.

func scanningUnique(_ ids: [String]) -> [String] {
    var output: [String] = []
    for id in ids where !output.contains(id) { output.append(id) }
    return output
}
func indexedUnique(_ ids: [String]) -> [String] {
    var seen: Set<String> = []
    var output: [String] = []
    for id in ids {
        if seen.insert(id).inserted { output.append(id) }
    }
    return output
}

for ... where filters loop entries without creating another output collection. Set<String> gives a membership index. insert returns a tuple whose inserted field reports whether this key was new. Both methods append in input traversal order; neither sorts or changes case. The candidate still hashes strings, allocates storage, and may increase transient memory by holding both arrays and a set.

Keep outputs observable so optimized compilation cannot discard the experiment. Construct fixtures outside a mapping-only interval, verify full arrays separately, and retain raw samples under the same build configuration. Add an allocation/peak-memory investigation if that is a meaningful budget. A faster mapping result supports a claim about that mapping boundary, while end-to-end latency, UI hitches, and energy remain separate experiments. Algorithm improvement often removes work more simply than extra tasks, but it must preserve all observable behavior.

sections.title: Write the benefit and the cost in the same decision
sections.html:
A decision record tells another engineer what changed and why the evidence supports it. Include the measured boundary, candidate, behavior checks, before-and-after samples, memory impact, configuration, and limits. For a type-checking rewrite, report build latency separately from runtime equivalence. For an algorithm change, report growth with input size and extra storage. For a module split, include dependencies, public surface, rebuild effects, and integration cost. These outcomes cannot be reduced to one useful optimization score. Choose the tradeoff for the problem you actually measured.

A small local result may justify further measurement rather than a production change. Reproduce unexplained regressions before adjusting the budget. If a candidate reduces compile time by exposing unstable implementation across modules, its maintenance cost may outweigh the benefit. If it increases peak memory during launch, a mapping speed gain may be unacceptable on representative devices. State the tradeoff and the unanswered question clearly, then choose the next experiment that resolves it.

Android boundaries matter here too: Swift's value semantics, ARC, generic specialization, result builders, and SPM products do not follow every Kotlin/JVM or Gradle rule. Use familiar build timelines and Big-O reasoning as starting tools, then inspect actual Swift constraints. Specialist compiler engineering, linker/ABI work, and large build-graph redesign remain further practice. This course teaches targeted source diagnosis and reproducible decisions; it does not claim that changing an annotation or adding modules always makes the build or app faster.

Yes, if Package.resolved exists.

quiz.question: Why can summed build-task durations exceed wall-clock build time?
options: The log must be corrupt.
Linking subtracts time from compilation.
Independent tasks overlap; the dependency critical path determines elapsed time.
quiz.explanation: Parallel task time is not the same quantity as elapsed build time. Inspect the timeline and dependency chain.

Return Array(Set(ids)) and assume insertion order.
Lowercase every identifier so there are fewer distinct values.
quiz.explanation: The input traversal preserves first-occurrence order. Unordered conversion and normalization can change visible behavior.

exercise.brief: Prepare separate investigations for a typed-expression rewrite and stable deduplication. Check behavior before measuring builds or runtime.
steps: Define a clean build, a build with no input changes, and an incremental build after one specified file edit. Preserve shared developer caches.
Explain rankedIDs' ordering, temporary arrays, and type inference.
Compare full results from scanningUnique and indexedUnique for empty, repeated, ordered mixed, and long Unicode-string inputs.
Plan several input sizes and memory checks. Name the additional screen-level evidence needed for a user-impact claim.
acceptance: Both uniqueness functions produce identical full ordered output for the declared fixtures.
Build and runtime performance are reported in separate sections with effective configuration and tool versions.
Input construction is excluded only from a clearly named mapping-only measurement.
Expected complexity and theoretical memory tradeoffs are not reported as observed improvements.
exercise.solution:
Both functions must turn ["b", "a", "b", "c"] into ["b", "a", "c"]. Compare the complete arrays, including order. Also try no items, all equal IDs, all distinct IDs, and mixed Unicode strings under the same Swift String equality rule. For rankedIDs, confirm that ties use ID order and nonpositive scores are omitted. Keep correctness assertions outside the timed block for both candidates. Timing only one version's assertions would make the comparison answer a different question.

The build sheet has independent no-op, private implementation edit, and public contract edit scenarios. Retain the same toolchain, host, destination, resolved dependencies, and declared output/cache preparation. Read timing summaries and the build timeline to identify type checking, dependency emission, linking, resources, or scripts. A source annotation change is a candidate, not a proven improvement.

The runtime sheet uses fixed datasets at several sizes, matched release configuration, observable results, and alternating baseline/candidate batches. Record raw times, sample count, median, p95 estimator, range, and allocation or peak evidence. Leave all observations pending until actual execution. The conditional conclusion is: “The membership model predicts less repeated searching with extra storage; device measurements must confirm the mapping tradeoff and a separate screen experiment must establish user impact.” This answer demonstrates contracts and reasoning without pre-completing the learner's profiling work.

lessons.title: Profiling lab: make one change and leave evidence others can check
lessons.summary: Compare one bounded change under matching conditions. Check correct behavior first, keep raw samples and traces, and write regression rules with honest limits.
objectives: Build a controlled synthetic workload with separate mapping and whole-user-operation boundaries.
Collect matched samples and diagnostic traces while accounting for profiler overhead.
Define correctness-first rules using device-group budgets and observed measurement noise.
Write a reproducible handoff that separates measured results, source reasoning, and work still pending.

sections.title: Choose one question the workload can answer
sections.html:
A workload is the chosen set of operations and inputs used in an experiment. This lab uses two levels: a small mapping benchmark and a whole UI flow. Android benchmarks and workflow tests offer the same useful separation, but the iOS tools and boundaries differ. In a separate Apple-platform scratch target, create results with stable IDs, text, and local image fixtures. Use an injected fake transport or bounded local test fixture. Synthetic means invented data. Do not send production searches or use patient data. The client anchors are source comparisons, not files to change.

Select one primary hypothesis, such as “Repeated row projection on MainActor causes commit hitches during scrolling.” Include a competing explanation, such as “Deferred image decoding dominates the same interval.” A lab with twenty simultaneous changes cannot identify which mechanism mattered. Keep a baseline, change one relevant boundary, and retain a straightforward way to run each version. The synthetic screen should exercise the cost at realistic data sizes while making output easy to verify.

Define launch to first frame, launch to usable content, projection time, gesture hitch evidence, transient decode peak, retained route-exit population, request/queue activity, and optional energy observation as distinct fields. Choose a primary success metric and guardrails before execution. A faster projection cannot alone establish faster launch or lower energy. The lab's outcome is a reviewable investigation, including honest incomplete evidence when a required device or tool is unavailable.

sections.title: Freeze inputs and choose a small set of conditions
sections.html:
A fixture revision names the exact data used for both versions. Keep row count, duplicate rate, string lengths, sort rule, image dimensions and orientation, pixel requests, payload limits, and fake completion schedule fixed. Use synthetic IDs and include insertion and reorder checks. Tiny ASCII labels and one square photo miss important layout and decoding limits. Add edge-case fixtures separately. Do not change the timed dataset silently between baseline and candidate. A comparison matrix lists the declared conditions you intend to run, including which remain pending.

Pick representative physical-device cohorts, ideally including a supported constrained device and a device/display condition relevant to high-refresh scrolling. Keep OS/build and configuration explicit. Also maintain a controlled simulator condition for functional checks and repeatable CI comparison, with its own baseline. Results from different phone models, OS versions, simulator hosts, or optimization configurations must not be merged as though they describe one identical environment.

Bound the matrix to questions you can answer: terminated-process versus resume, declared warm/cold image data, a small set of concurrency limits, and the chosen baseline/candidate. A full cross-product can become too large and hide the primary comparison. Treat first-install or migration paths as separate fixtures if relevant. Record which matrix cells ran and which remain pending. Installation and process preparation are procedures, not magic switches that guarantee all OS state was reset.

sections.title: Reject a wrong answer before timing it
sections.html:
A correctness invariant is a behavior rule that must hold for every accepted result. Check output order, duplicates, row IDs, image orientation and dimensions, selection, larger text, and loading or error state before comparing speed. A version that drops difficult rows or shows old photos may look faster while being wrong. Include empty and corrupt inputs. Keep cancellation distinct from success. A cancelled or partial operation must not be labeled successful content merely because it completed quickly.

Use gated fakes to test interleavings. Hold work, replace the query or leave the screen, then release the gate and verify the old result cannot publish. For shared caching, distinguish a waiter stopping from the service-owned operation stopping. On logout, assert old generations cannot repopulate the account cache and that visible state cannot commit old account results. A hundred sleep-based repetitions are less informative than controlling the precise race you need to verify.

After those functional invariants pass, keep expensive correctness checks outside the measured inner block and inspect results afterward. Do not bypass middleware, protections, or availability branches merely to improve timing. Read the effective compiler and deployment settings for every test target; a scratch macro or API compiling on your Mac does not establish it compiles in the app's configured iOS destination. Keep behavioral evidence, compiler checks, and performance observations as separate claims.

sections.title: Use a short trace to explain the cause
sections.html:
A diagnostic run records detail to help explain a mechanism. Mark projection, image decode, and usable-content intervals with signposts. Record the Instruments version and template. For a suspected commit hitch, select the missed app deadline and inspect synchronous main-thread work. For a render hitch, inspect rendering and compositing. With supported Instruments 26 and runtime, inspect SwiftUI body and representable updates. A representable is a UIKit bridge in SwiftUI. Tool colors and thresholds help classify work; they are not universal frame-time budgets.

For memory, compare allocation generations across repeated route entry/exit and inspect the retained ownership graph. Separately examine transient peak during overlapping decodes. A steady population is not enough if peak remains unsafe. For network/I/O, separate provider work, transfer, parsing, caching, and disk writes. Record actual queued/active work and termination paths rather than inferring a limit from the presence of a task group.

Save the trace, revision, matching symbols, selected interval, and notes explaining what the evidence supports. A screenshot can help navigation, but the underlying trace lets a reviewer inspect another stack or interval. Instrumentation adds overhead, so these diagnostic observations primarily explain causes. Confirm the primary metric with equivalent minimally instrumented runs. No trace was recorded merely because you opened repository files or authored signpost code; mark that phase pending until it actually happens.

sections.title: Keep raw observations under a rule chosen in advance
sections.html:
A sampling plan states how runs are prepared, counted, and summarized before results arrive. Define estimator, warm-up handling, outcome categories, and invalid-run rules. Ten iterations can expose harness mistakes but offer weak p95 evidence. A larger matched batch, such as one hundred successful observations per device group, offers more tail information without guaranteeing statistical certainty. Cohort means a group with comparable device and environment conditions. Pick sample counts for the decision, keep raw order, and report failures and uncertainty rather than promising precision from a convenient number.

Alternate or randomize baseline and candidate in matched batches to reduce time and thermal drift. Keep the original sample order as well as sorted values. Record failure, cancellation, timeout, bad preparation, and thermal changes. Do not remove slow runs after seeing the answer. If preparation violates a predeclared rule, retain that fact and rerun the same way for both versions. A timed-out async test is not a completed latency sample.

Report count, median, p95 estimator, range, units, and cohort conditions. Inspect whether the same phase dominates the slow samples rather than adding independent phase percentiles. Repeated measurements on one device are not a fleet distribution. Bootstrap or another confidence method can support a specialist analysis when its assumptions are understood; printing a p95 with many decimal places cannot provide that confidence by itself.

sections.title: Check what the test harness actually times
sections.html:
A harness is the test code that prepares inputs, runs work, and records output. Add lesson 041's uniqueness functions to a separate XCTest target before using this example. Its fixture is prepared outside the measurement, so it times mapping only. The test does not automatically choose an iOS destination or produce raw p95 observations. Read the runner's result records and options before naming the boundary. A compiling test and a source comment are not evidence of an executed benchmark.

import XCTest

final class ScratchMappingTests: XCTestCase {
    func testMappingMetric() {
        let input = (0..<10_000).map { "id-\($0 % 2_000)" }
        let expected = (0..<2_000).map { "id-\($0)" }
        let options = XCTMeasureOptions()
        options.iterationCount = 20
        var last: [String] = []
        measure(metrics: [XCTClockMetric()], options: options) {
            last = indexedUnique(input)
        }
        XCTAssertEqual(last, expected)
    }
}

The modulo expression intentionally repeats two thousand IDs, making the fixture deterministic. Expected output preserves first occurrence. The result is inspected, and the same harness must be used for a baseline. Twenty requested iterations demonstrate setup; inspect actual result records and the runner's options before computing percentiles. An aggregate XCTest summary is not equivalent to a retained raw-sample dataset.

The active networking benchmark creates/consumes streams inside measure and waits for expectations. Read the wait result and failure behavior: completion, timeout, and a child error can change what the interval means. The checked-in benchmark plan lists nonparallel targets and the shared scheme references it, which supports active configuration evidence. It does not prove CI executes that plan or that anyone measured the source comment's proposed threshold. Inspect the selected test plan and result bundle when making those claims.

sections.title: Make each failing rule lead to an action
sections.html:
A regression gate is a declared rule for accepting or investigating a change. First reject incorrect behavior. Then use separate budgets for the specific mapping fixture, device launch readiness, fixed-gesture hitches, and route-cycle memory peak or retention. Choose budgets from baseline observations and product needs, with measurement variation and useful effect size in mind. A threshold invented after seeing the candidate is not a fair gate. State who owns each budget and how a justified update is reviewed.

A paired control can help reveal drift on a noisy runner. An absolute budget expresses a user requirement. Both need review if the environment or fixture changes. Keep simulator CI and physical-device release baselines separate. Save raw artifacts so a reviewer can distinguish a real regression from a broken harness or disturbed runner. Investigate unexplained failures under a declared rerun rule; do not automatically loosen the threshold or retry without limit.

Use a gate that has an actionable outcome: inspect evidence, revert the bounded candidate, or escalate a new bottleneck. Avoid unbounded retries until a run passes. Require confirmation after any new implementation change or unexpected finding, but do not repeat every expensive experiment when no relevant input changed. Build/runtime/memory/energy checks have different costs; choose the smallest set that detects the stated risk while retaining device evidence for conclusions that depend on hardware.

The regression-decisions workshop provides a runnable JavaScript evaluator in MeasurementLab. Its labeled synthetic records exercise pass, regression, invalid preparation, and missing data, with correctness, comparable cohorts, raw outcomes, and declared nearest-rank p95 checked before budget decisions. Those fixture values are not suggested product budgets. Replace them only through an agreed experiment contract, preserve the original data, and keep device, rendering, and energy evidence in their own rows.

sections.title: Give another engineer enough to replay the claim
sections.html:
A handoff is the record another engineer needs to inspect and repeat the work. Lead with the change, reason, behavior checks, measured operation, and comparison under matching conditions. Include raw samples, estimator, count, phone and OS, tools, effective configuration, cache preparation, trace intervals, and artifact locations. Label a source-derived hypothesis as a hypothesis and pixel arithmetic as an estimate. Keep compiler timing in its own build context. An unrun device check stays pending; it must not become an observed improvement in the report.

State unresolved work precisely. If only a simulator mapping test ran, first usable frame and physical-device energy remain unverified. If a trace shows render-server complexity, advanced compositing or Metal work may require a specialist. Memory-pressure termination diagnostics, statistical confidence, compiler/linker internals, and fleet telemetry each deserve additional practice when they determine the decision. Do not call the course exhaustive or claim a source audit has completed profiling.

A worked answer can provide report structure and correct helper code without filling in the learner's observations. Keep pending exercises pending. The mentor standard is that another engineer can reproduce your claim, challenge its assumptions, and know exactly which next measurement would resolve uncertainty. That is also the strongest bridge from mature Android performance practice: mechanism, ownership, controlled conditions, and evidence travel well, while each platform's runtime and tool details still require direct inspection.

quiz.question: A candidate has fewer items because it silently drops failures. Can lower latency pass the gate?
options: Yes, fewer items are always cheaper.
Only if the trace looks smooth.
No, correctness and outcome classification must pass before performance comparison.
quiz.explanation: A changed output/failure contract is not a valid optimization of the original operation. Preserve failures and partial-success policy explicitly.

quiz.question: What establishes that the active benchmark plan actually executed?
options: A source comment naming the plan.
Selected runner/plan evidence and retained execution results.
The mere presence of a benchmark target in Package.swift.
quiz.explanation: Manifest and scheme evidence show configuration. Actual execution needs runner selection and result artifacts, not source presence alone.

quiz.question: A simulator mapping metric passes. What remains unverified?
options: Physical-device launch, smoothness, memory pressure, and energy conclusions outside that boundary.
Nothing; simulators represent every supported phone.
Only the spelling of the metric name.
quiz.explanation: A narrow controlled metric detects that boundary's behavior. Device-specific product performance requires the relevant device experiments.

exercise.brief: Investigate one bounded synthetic change and propose regression rules. Keep any measurement you have not run clearly marked pending.
steps: Freeze both versions, fixture revision, main hypothesis, behavior rules, and comparison conditions.
Prepare a mapping XCTest harness, signposted UI operation, repeatable gesture, and memory entry-exit cycle in a scratch target.
Run available checks. When tools and device permit, save diagnostic traces and matched raw samples with minimal instrumentation.
Summarize each cohort using the declared rule. Keep failures and explain phase costs without adding unrelated p95 values.
Write correctness-first gates, artifact locations, rollback condition, owners, and precise unresolved specialist work.
acceptance: Each claim is labeled measured, source-derived, theoretical, or pending.
Observed results include raw samples, sample count, estimator, matching environment, and correctness evidence.
No simulator result certifies phone rendering, memory pressure, or energy.
A timeout/unfinished async task cannot silently become a completed latency sample.
Gate policy uses observed variance and user relevance, with a bounded failure/review action.
The lab leaves client source and learner completion state unchanged.
exercise.solution:
This worked investigation moves one unchanged row projection from repeated view evaluation to the accepted data-revision boundary. First check order, equality, empty and error state, insertion and reorder identity, and cancellation. The hypothesis is less redundant synchronous main-thread work. Image decoding and rendering remain competing explanations. The answer supplies a design and report structure, not observed candidate timing. The learner still builds the workload, runs the available checks, and records any device evidence.

The report records a frozen synthetic fixture and separate simulator and physical-device cohorts. Its raw table has revision, cohort, sample index, outcome, preparation, total operation time, projection time, cache state, and thermal notes. Summary fields contain n, median, nearest-rank p95, range, failures, and conditions only after collection. A diagnostic trace identifies selected intervals and attribution; an equivalent minimal-instrumentation batch confirms the primary operation. A memory sheet separates pixel estimates, transient peak, and route-exit retention. An energy sheet stays pending until supported device observations exist.

The gate proposal says: “Reject incorrect or stale output first. For the declared fixture/cohort, compare the candidate with the established usability and hitch budgets and the paired baseline distribution. Preserve raw artifacts. If the result fails or the effect is within unexplained noise, inspect/reproduce under the same protocol; do not automatically relax thresholds. Revert the isolated candidate when its measured regression is established.” Numeric budgets are filled from real baseline data and product requirements, not guessed here.

The handoff lists benchmark target, selected plan/runner, command and tool versions, result bundle, trace, fixture, and preparation procedure. It states whether any code merely type-checked, tests actually ran, or device profiling actually happened. A peer should be able to replay one cohort without asking what “warm” meant. If hardware is unavailable, the completed artifact is a validated design with pending device evidence, not a fabricated performance improvement. The learner still performs and records the experiment.
